title: Which price is least, and how do you order all six?
description: Tanvi reads six price tags in an electric bike shop. The video orders them from least to greatest, comparing from the left.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number with a bigger leftmost digit is greater, and equal leftmost digits send you to the next place. Watch for thinking a long run of nines beats a number that starts with a bigger digit.

source: Let Us Do (second set) 4, prices of electric bikes
video_script.why: The child can order a short list but meets prices that are very close, like eighty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine and ninety thousand.
video_script.substitution: Sort by the ten thousands digit, then compare the thousands inside the group that matches.
video_script.anchor: Tanvi reading price tags in an electric bike shop
video_script.wrong_answer: eighty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine is greater than ninety thousand, because it has so many nines
video_script.wrong_move: Chintu puts eighty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine after ninety thousand, because it has so many nines. But eight ten thousands is less than nine ten thousands.
video_script.payoff_line: the six prices are now in order from least to greatest

final_answer.spoken: thirty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, forty-nine thousand nine hundred, eighty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine, ninety thousand, ninety-three thousand seven hundred and forty-three and ninety-four thousand nine hundred and eighty-three

maths_rules: ten thousands digits: 9, 8, 9, 4, 9, 3; so 39,999 (3) < 49,900 (4) < 89,999 (8) < the three prices that start with 9
video_script.design: Exercise: order six five digit prices. Hint: the ten thousands digit first. The six tags stay on the stage and the sorted row is built below them.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='shop'/>Tanvi visits a shop that sells electric bikes. Six price tags hang on the bikes.
<bookmark mark='a'/>The tags show ninety thousand, and eighty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.
<bookmark mark='b'/>Two more show ninety-four thousand, nine hundred and eighty-three, and forty-nine thousand, nine hundred.
<bookmark mark='c'/>The last two show ninety-three thousand, seven hundred and forty-three, and thirty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Put the prices in ascending order, least first.

narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='chintu'/>Eighty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine is greater than ninety thousand, because it has so many nines.
<bookmark mark='nines'/>He counted the nines and did not look at the biggest place.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>Eight ten thousands is less than nine ten thousands. Adding one more rupee to eighty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine gives ninety thousand.

narration: <bookmark mark='low'/>Look at the ten thousands digits. Three is the least, then four, then eight.
<bookmark mark='three'/>These are thirty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine, and forty-nine thousand, nine hundred. Then comes eighty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.

<bookmark mark='order'/>Zero is the least, then three, then four.

<bookmark mark='rule'/>If the digits match, look at the next place to the right.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Does each price in your row come before a greater one?
